title: Jonah's Great Fish
lead: "The LORD appointed a huge fish to swallow Jonah" (Jonah 1:17), and after three days and nights "It vomited Jonah onto the dry land" (Jonah 2:10). The Hebrew says only "a great fish"; the "whale" comes from the KJV's wording of Jesus' saying in Matthew 12:40, where the Greek ketos means a sea monster. Jesus made Jonah's three days in the fish the sign of his own death and rising.

sections.b: Jonah calls it dag gadol, "a great fish" (Jonah 1:17), and simply dag, "fish," when the LORD speaks to it (Jonah 2:10); in Jonah 2:1 the word is the feminine dagah. The book never says what kind of creature it was. The key verb is "appointed" (Hebrew vayman): God appoints the fish, then a plant, a worm and a hot east wind (Jonah 4:6–8). The sea, the fish, the plant and the worm all obey at once; only the prophet runs. Inside the fish Jonah prays (Jonah 2:1), and his prayer says, "From the belly of Sheol I cried for help" (Jonah 2:2): the fish is the place where he is as good as dead, and also the means by which God saves him.

The Septuagint renders the great fish as ketos mega, "a great sea creature" (Jonah 2:1 in its numbering), and Matthew uses the same word when Jesus says, "Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster" (Matthew 12:40). The STEPBible lexicon defines ketos as "a huge fish, sea-monster"; the Greek Bible uses it for the great sea creatures of Genesis 1:21 too. The KJV turned it into "the whale's belly" in Matthew, while keeping "a great fish" in Jonah, and the Latin Vulgate has piscem grandem, "a great fish." So "Jonah and the whale" is an English tradition, not the wording of the Hebrew or the Greek.

Jewish tradition took the fish as real and wonderful. In Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 10, Rabbi Tarfon says the fish was appointed from the six days of creation to swallow Jonah; its two eyes were like windows giving him light, and it showed him the depths of the sea and even Leviathan. Rashi, following that tradition, explains the feminine dagah in Jonah 2:1: Jonah had room in a male fish and did not pray, so God moved him into a crowded female fish, and there he prayed. Christian tradition also took it as a miracle. When pagans laughed at the story, Augustine answered that anyone who believes Christ rose on the third day has no reason to doubt it, and pointed to the huge ribs of a sea creature on public display in Carthage (Letter 102, AD 409). Jesus himself treats it as the sign for his generation: "Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster. In the same way the Son of Man will spend three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" (Matthew 12:40). Many modern scholars read the book of Jonah as a teaching story or parable, so that the fish belongs to the story's message rather than to a report of events; the Jonah page sets out that debate. Either way, the fish serves the book's point: the LORD rules the sea and has mercy on whom he chooses, even a runaway prophet.
